sm: The program opens on Friday, November 13th with hosts Myrna Brown and Nick Eicher. Kent Covington reports that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang stepped down amid reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a businesswoman suspected of spying for China. Attorney General Todd Blanche confirmed an investigation, and investigators are examining whether a related company helped smuggle restricted computer chips into China. Chief financial officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO. Other stories include a U.S. warning that Israel should prepare for possible renewed fighting with Iran, and a Trump threat to double tariffs on Mexico over a migrant caravan. Weekly jobless claims held near 200,000, and a gunman killed one person and wounded four at a Washington gym before killing himself.

John Stonestreet of the Colson Center joins the hosts for Culture Friday. They discuss parents suing schools over grades, including a mother who went to court over a third grader's comment about cooperation. Stonestreet says conflicts with teachers are common, but taking a dispute to court instead of talking face to face is not where the court should be. He also notes that telling a student's own work from AI work will be a lasting problem. The hosts then raise comedian Billy Crystal saying he does not trust God after his losses. Stonestreet says Job's friends did best when they simply sat with him, and that the Christian answer to suffering is that Jesus came and wept with us.

Stonestreet and the hosts turn to the Nvidia story. He calls it a reminder of the importance of private character, and recalls Chuck Colson saying that people have an unlimited capacity for self-rationalization. They then discuss President Trump's 60 Minutes interview, especially his comments on forgiveness. Stonestreet says forgiveness is difficult for everyone, and that he credits the president for not pretending otherwise. He says the Bible ties forgiving others to having been forgiven, and notes that the topic captivated viewers, which says something about the spiritual climate. The hosts thank him and say goodbye until next week.

Nick Eicher and Myrna Brown introduce a segment on the new film Ebenezer, with arts editor Colin Garbarino reporting. Johnny Depp stars as Ebenezer Scrooge, with Rupert Grant as Bob Cratchit and Ian McKellen as Jacob Marley, in a surprisingly faithful adaptation by director Ty West. The reviewer praises the Dickensian sets and costumes, and Depp's whimsical but cranky performance. He notes the film keeps the Christian themes, adding scenes of church attendance and a singing of Silent Night. It is rated PG-13, and because the director mostly works in horror, the ghosts are frightening and may be too scary for small children.

The final segment features musician Phil Madeira and his new album, The Millionth Mile, reported by Arsenio Orteza. Madeira began with the Phil Keaggy Band, wrote songs recorded by artists including Garth Brooks and Toby Keith, and has toured about eighteen years with Emmylou Harris. He recorded his own version of If I Was Jesus, which Keith had recorded in 2003. He says he likes writing with others because it gives songs wider appeal, and he also wrote songs on slavery's lingering effects and a preacher struggling with drinking. He credits his Baptist preacher father as his tether to Christianity. The program closes with the production credits.
